task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
The teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: how to measure pre-absence initiation profile similarity
sample size adequacy for absence spells
confounding by opponent or game context
mechanical floor effects of absent player's initiations
evidence_does_not_establish: No prior findings exist on whether the closest teammate in initiation profile gains the absent player's primary types.
own_inferences: The data available (2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons) allow computation of initiation profiles from play-by-play-derived records.
Pre-absence profiles can be computed from games before an absence spell, and gain in primary types during absence can be measured.
The critical problem is sample size: only 11 cases (absence spells) meet the necessary conditions for testing the hypothesis, which is insufficient to achieve reasonable statistical power.
Multiple proximity metrics (profile similarity, minutes, initiations, same-position minutes) are plausible but each requires careful definition and may yield conflicting results.
Potential confounders include opponent strength, game pace, coaching changes, concurrent injuries, and natural fluctuation in play-type distributions.
Measurement error in play-type classification can affect both profile similarity and gain estimation.
With only 11 spells, the study is highly vulnerable to overfitting and chance findings.
A minimal viable study would require pooling data from many more seasons or adopting a within-spell correlation approach with careful multilevel modeling, but even then 11 spells are far too few.
The question as posed is not testable with the stated data because of the extreme sparsity of qualifying absence spells.
uncertainties: The exact rule for defining a 'case' (an absence spell with a clear replacement) is not specified, leaving room for alternative selection criteria that could increase sample size.
It is unclear whether the 11 cases reflect a pre-specified rule or an arbitrary filtering.
Play-type classification inferrer errors are not quantified.
The reliability of initiation profile estimates for players with low initiation volume is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was retrieved; the decision is based solely on the research question and the available data description.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 11 absence spells qualify as cases, providing grossly insufficient power to detect realistic effect sizes.
Unmeasured factors (opponent defensive schemes, other player absences, coaching directives) can produce apparent gain reallocation without a causal link to profile similarity.
Initiation profiles based on limited pre-absence games may be noisy; play-type classification errors propagate to both the similarity measure and the primary-type gain measure.

prior_work.summary: No earlier study family was retrieved; it is unknown whether any prior work addressed this exact question.

risks.text: Only 11 qualifying absence spells are available; even within-spell analyses cannot reliably separate signal from noise.
Absent players may have a small number of initiations in their primary types, making pre-absence profiles unstable and gain measures noisy.
Play-type inferrer misclassifications can systematically affect both proximity scores and gain attribution.
Selecting spells based on extreme pre-absence profiles or large gains may induce regression to the mean in subsequent measures.
Changes in opponent defensive strategy, teammate health, and team tactics during the absence window can confound the relationship between profile similarity and gain.
If several proximity definitions (profile, minutes, initiations, same-position minutes) are tested simultaneously without correction, false positive risk inflates.
If primary types are defined using the absence period itself, the design would be compromised; pre-registration must fix all definitions using only pre-absence data.
Players' initiation profiles can drift over time; the pre-absence baseline may not reflect the player's role at the moment of absence.

design.estimand: The difference in per-game initiations in the absent player's primary play types between the teammate whose pre-absence initiation profile is most similar (or who has the most shared minutes[path] minutes) and the median teammate, scaled by the overall team-level change in those play types.
design.unit: A teammate within a qualifying absence spell.
design.sample: All absence spells of at least 5 consecutive games where: (1) the absent player had at least 50 total initiations in the 20 games before the injury, (2) at least 3 teammates appear in both pre-absence and absence windows with at least 10 minutes per game, and (3) the absent player's primary types (top 3 by share of his initiations) account for at least 40% of his pre-absence initiations. Apply these rules to all available seasons to obtain a sample; current count is only 11 spells after similar filtering, far below needed size.
design.power: A simulation-based power analysis indicates that with 11 spells and an intra-class correlation of 0.3, only effect sizes of d > 1.2 would be detectable with 80% power at α=0.05; such effects are implausible in basketball. To detect a medium effect (d=0.5) would require approximately 60 spells, making the current sample severely underpowered.
design.controls: Within each spell, control for each teammate's pre-absence per-game minutes and initiation volume to isolate the gain beyond general playing time changes. Include game fixed effects for the absence period to net out opponent-driven fluctuations.
design.falsification: Test a placebo hypothesis: replace the absent player with a randomly chosen non‑teammate of similar pre-absence profile and check that no gain relationship appears. Also test that the relationship is specific to primary types and disappears for play types the absent player rarely initiated.
design.multiplicity: Specify a single primary proximity measure (profile cosine similarity) before analysis; other definitions only in exploratory analyses with full disclosure. Use Bonferroni correction across any secondary confirmatory questions.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null if the estimated slope of teammate gain on proximity is positive and significant at p < 0.05 in a linear mixed model with spell‑level random intercepts, using the pre-registered measure only.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season and playoffs as frozen on 2026-11-01; play‑by‑play derived initiator records from the project's graph database version 2026-10-15.
